                           Spotted glaze utilizing plaster (Calcium sulfate) to induce spotting at Cone 6 due to
                           bubbles formed during firing.


                             This was inspired by TheHeartlessMachine's use of Epsom salts (Magnesium sulfate) to
                            achieve frothing in Locke's Residue. Magnesium sulfate will also achieve spotting when
                         used in similar weight amounts as the Calcium sulfate used in this recipe.
                                                                                               △6 Oxidation
                           Layering                                                                Wind Breaker stained with blue stain,
                                                                                                                followed by White Cover 4.1, fired to
                                                    I brush on several coats of the WindBreaker base glaze followed by a contrasting color
                                                                                            Cone 6 Medium speed.
                          Cover glaze.

                                                                                                                                                        Kevin Matocha
                      One example of a Cover glaze is White Cover 4.1 (https://glazy.org/recipes/714396), but                1 month ago
                       many other Cover glazes have been successful.


                            Stains and other colorants
                                                    I have observed success with many stain types. If using an encapsulated stain
                          (sometimes called inclusion stains), consider adding 3% Zirconium silicate to your recipe
                              to reduce frothing. (See detailed discussion of zirconia and encapsulated stains in Color
                          Spotted Base.


                                  In addition to stains, some other colorants may work. I have also used an opacifier (such
                           as Zirconium silicate) followed by a color-stained Cover to achieve white spots in a
                             colored background.


                              Application thickness strongly impacts spot sizes.


                             Generally delivers a smooth, glossy surface.


                             Plaster
                            "Old" casting plaster was ground with mortar and pestle and added to mix. Mix was then
                             sieved with 100 mesh screen. If you use "fresh" plaster, I recommend to use about half as
                      much as recommended in this recipe. Due to the strong hygroscopic nature of plaster, the
                              "old" plaster tends to pick up water, thus weighs more for the same amount of Calcium
                                 sulfate.


                            For a brushing glaze, Mix with 25g CMC gum mix (4% concentration) and approximately
                       45g of water.

                                                                                                         Julie Lee
                                                                          3 days ago

                                                                  Nice work, thank you for sharing! Can't wait to try this out.
                                                                       This might be a silly question, but when you say you crushed
                                                                        old plaster with mortar and pestle, do you mean you crushed
                                                               formed plaster, or it was just old and chunky in the bag?



                                                                                           Kevin Matocha
                                                                          3 days ago

                                                              Thanks for the question and clarification. For this recipe I use
                                                                             plaster straight from the bag. By “old” I mean a bag of plaster
                                                                            that has been sitting open for too long, thus absorbing
                                                                     moisture from the atmosphere and no longer useful for
                                                              making molds. It has absorbed moisture and sometimes gets
                                                                    chunky, contrasting with “fresh” plaster that is powdery. So
                                                                           usually run the mortar/pestle to break up the “old” plaster
                                                               chunks and it leaves a more powdery consistency again.


                                                                     Also I sieve my mixtures to eliminate any remaining plaster
                                                                    chunks.
